https://www.dw.com/en/italy-etna-eruptio.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IhLR Etna is Europe's most active volcano and has disrupted flights into Sicily several times in recent years Image: Etna Walk/AFP Advertisement Sicily's Catania airport on Wednesday suspended flights until at least 4 p.m. local time (1400 GMT/UTC) on Thursday, responding to fresh ash emissions from Mount Etna . The volcanic ash can pose a danger to aircraft and so has forced regulators to restrict access to the airspace around eastern Sicily, disrupting the peak summer holiday season. Where were flights affected? "Passengers are advised to check the status of their flights with their airlines," airport operator SAC said. "Further updates will follow in the coming hours." Catania airport flights have faced disruptions since late last week, becoming more intense as the eruption continues Image: Darrin Zammit Lupi/REUTERS Travel disruptions have impacted eastern Sicily in particular since last Friday, when renewed rumblings from Europe's most active volcano and shifting winds started carrying ash over the region. The airspace was fully closed only in recent days as the eruption continued. The prolonged restrictions at Catania — on Sicily's eastern coast just south of Mount Etna — have placed extra strain on Sicily's other airports during one of the busiest seasons for vacationers. Palermo Mayor Roberto Lagalla said that his city's airport had taken in around 190 flights originally scheduled to land on the eastern side of the island in recent days. For milennia, the port of Catania has sat in the foothills of Mount Etna, sometimes facing severe disruption or even damage from its eruptions Image: Giuseppe Di Stefano/Etna Walk/REUTERS Italy 's ANSA news agency also reported on Wednesday that flights were resuming at Comiso airport, a smaller hub south of Catania, after it had suspended traffic late on Tuesday. Some of the volcanic ash was also drifting south across the Mediterranean towards Malta, which had reported significant delays and some cancellations. On Wednesday, Malta International Airport continued to warn passengers of possible disruptions but said that conditions were improving. What is Mount Etna? Mount Etna is a roughly 3,400 meter (roughly 11,100 feet) stratovolcano on Sicily's eastern coast. Its precise height is ever changing, particularly amid periods of high activity when it can shed a few meters. The city of Catania is located not far to the south. Volcanic activity can lead to particularly fertile soils and other benefits that explain why cities like Catania were built so close to mountains like Etna Image: Etna Walk/AFP It is one of the tallest active volcanoes in Europe and Italy's highest peak south of the Alps. It's in an almost constant state of low-level activity and erupts in a more pronounced manner fairly frequently. It has caused disruptions at Catania airport several times in recent years . A UNESCO World Heritage Site, the first volcanic activity took place at Etna about half a million years ago. Both Roman and Greek mythology asserted that the god of blacksmithing — either Vulcan or Hephaestus — had his forge beneath Mount Etna. Roman poet Virgil wrote about an eruption at Etna in his epic poem the Aeneid, in what's thought to be a first-hand account Image: Etna Walk/AFP Edited by: Louis Oelofse If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google , so you'll always see our verified news first. Photograph: Sarah Rice/Bloomberg via Getty Images Trump administration Trump EPA aims to exempt datacenters from disclosing air pollution, advocates warn Trump administration proposes new rule to dismantle requirement for datacenters to publicly report air pollution Tom Perkins Tue 25 Aug 2026 07.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A new rule proposed by the Trump administration aims to kill public notification for datacenter air pollution, public health advocates warn, and allow emission permits to be issued behind closed doors. The datacenters are often sources of nitrogen oxide, which helps form ozone, carbon monoxide and heavy metals, among other pollutants. The Clean Air Act requires “minor” air polluters to disclose to the public via state agencies how much pollution their proposed project will release, but the proposed new rule from Donald Trump’s Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) would dismantle that protection for datacenter proposals. Instead, it would make disclosure voluntary at state and some local officials’ discretion. Many state political establishments support datacenters, and observers say it is unlikely most would voluntarily require big tech to disclose the information. The move is likely intended to curb criticism and public oversight of datacenters, said Joe Goffman, a former assistant administrator for the EPA’s office of air and radiation. Without this data, communities won’t know what they’re breathing once a datacenter is built, and will have less ability to fight back in court or in public relations battles. Goffman said the Clean Air Act is supposed to offer “an ironclad promise” to give the entire US public a voice on these issues. “The administration is basically saying: ‘You all may have thought this was an ironclad promise, but it no longer is,’” Goffman added. He co-authored comments on the proposed rule submitted by the Environmental Protection Network. The EPA just closed the public comment period, and the rule could face a legal challenge if finalized. The move comes amid a national surge in datacenters that are an essential part of the artificial intelligence boom. Many datacenter developers apply for minor pollution source permits for the up to dozens of diesel generators or gas turbines used to help power their facilities, or provide backup generation. The EPA delegates monitoring of “minor” pollution sources to state authorities, while it handles major polluters like gas plants. The “minor” designation means that a company is proposing to put in enough pollution controls that it will not release a level of emissions that requires immediate federal oversight. The minor pollution permits are meant to ensure facilities follow federal limits on six pollutants linked to asthma, heart disease and cancer. Big tech often chops its datacenters pollution permit requests into individual pieces for each generator or turbine, so they fall under “minor” reviews conducted by states, and avoid a larger review by the EPA that would be more costly, time consuming and difficult to legally defend. This is already legally dubious, advocates say, and the Trump administration now appears to be trying to eliminate what little transparency exists. Though individual members of the public typically are not involved in the regulatory battles, environmental law clinics and public health advocacy groups that protect the public from exploitation by datacenter developers rely on this data, as do journalists. The Guardian last year detailed how environmental law groups have sued the state of Michigan and some polluters who appeared to be violating federal limits. Goffman said data shows that air pollution laws are more closely followed in areas in which the public and watchdog groups are more involved. Some of the largest polluting sources in the midwest, including datacenters, “emit harmful air pollutants under so-called ‘minor source’ permits”, said Jessica O’Donnell, senior attorney at the Environmental Law and Policy Center. “The public deserves to weigh in on such permits to ensure these industrial sources are given appropriate emissions limits and stick to them,” O’Donnell added. The EPA wrote that the change is “intended to reduce administrative burden and responsibly speed up permitting, supporting American economic development and energy dominance” by putting state agencies “most familiar with local issues in the driver’s seat”. A spokesperson for the EPA did not immediately send a comment. Goffman said the flexibility could also be wielded as an incentive for states competing for datacenter investment, and take the form of a “regulatory subsidy”. Datacenter developers often try to avoid scrutiny and regulation, so local and state governments eager to attract them could offer to waive the public notice. That concern is especially relevant as the Trump administration seeks to accelerate datacenter development by expanding opportunities for “islanded” power-generation facilities that provide their own power generation instead of connecting to the grid where their pollution is more closely scrutinized. “This proposal continues efforts by the current administration to turn its back on the fundamental EPA principle of transparency,” said Mike Koerber, a former deputy director of the EPA’s office of air quality planning and standards. Photograph: andresr/Getty Images View image in fullscreen The three bookmakers have repeatedly warned the government that excessive regulation or taxation could drive their customers into the arms of rogue offshore casinos. Photograph: andresr/Getty Images Gambling UK bookmakers that warned of rogue casinos profited from offshore gambling Content provider part-owned by Ladbrokes, William Hill and Betfred owner signed deal with Santeda network, Casino Secrets leak reveals Rob Davies Thu 1 Oct 2026 07.18 EDT First published on Thu 1 Oct 2026 05.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Three UK bookmakers that have repeatedly warned of the dangers of the illicit market have also benefited from a lucrative deal with one of the world’s largest offshore casinos, the Guardian can reveal. Details of the arrangement emerged as a result of last week’s Casino Secrets leak , which saw the release of thousands of confidential files held by the gambling regulator on the Caribbean island of Curaçao, a haven for offshore betting sites. One leaked file concerns the Santeda online casino network, which has been accused of illegally targeting vulnerable gamblers in the UK and has been fined in Spain for operating without a licence. The file shows that Santeda signed a deal in 2022 with Sports Information Services (SIS) – a UK-based gambling content provider part-owned by Ladbrokes, William Hill and Fred Done, the billionaire owner of Betfred. The three bookmakers have repeatedly warned the government that excessive regulation or taxation could drive their customers into the arms of rogue offshore casinos with no licence to operate in Britain. According to the leak, all three have also benefited from a share of tens of millions of pounds in dividends paid out by SIS after it signed the contract with Santeda. The companies are understood to have been unaware of the deal at the time it was signed. Matt Zarb-Cousin, a prominent gambling reform campaigner, advised them to get their “house in order”. The bookmakers collectively own more than 50% of SIS, which supplies gambling sites with live horse racing, greyhound and esports content, as well as data used to settle bets with customers. The use of such data is critical to online betting companies, helping them serve customers and process their bets. The leaked contract shows that SIS also agreed to provide Santeda websites with these services for two years, under a contract that auto-renewed unless either side opted to terminate it. Under the terms of the deal, SIS received a percentage of revenues from losing bets placed via Santeda’s brands. It is not clear whether the contract is still active, or how much SIS earned from it. SIS declined to say whether the deal had been terminated. Industry sources said that Ladbrokes, William Hill and Fred Done could not have known about the deal with Santeda, owing to controls designed to prevent them accessing commercially-sensitive information about industry rivals. One source said the companies were “furious” with SIS for doing business with Santeda, at a time when licensed operators were stepping up their warnings about the illicit market. Entain said it was “not a party to the commercial or customer arrangements SIS decides to strike. Now that this relationship has come to light, we take it very seriously and have raised our concerns to SIS”. The contract with Santeda does not permit the use of SIS data in the UK. But it appears to show that SIS supplied information to multiple Santeda websites that a previous Guardian investigation found was illegally targeting UK customers, including via promotional material apparently aimed at people trying to quit . Santeda’s Curaçao licence does not permit it to operate in most leading jurisdictions that regulate gambling, such as the UK and US. Companies House filings suggest that SIS’s shareholders – including Ladbrokes, William Hill and Done – have received at least £37m in dividends since the deal with Santeda was signed, including £30m in 2023. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning after newsletter promotion Ladbrokes owns 23% of SIS, suggesting it has received £8.5m in payouts over the period. Stella David, the chief executive of the Ladbrokes owner Entain, has criticised Premier League football clubs for “complicity” in fuelling illicit operators and warned that such firms could be boosted by any rise in taxes on licensed operators such as Ladbrokes. William Hill appears to have received more than £7m from its near-20% stake in SIS. Earlier this year, the bookmaker’s owner, Evoke, blamed the illicit market for weak online revenues. Fred Done, who is also a director of SIS, holds an 8% stake, indicating his share of shareholder payouts was nearly £3m. Done warned the chancellor this month that higher taxes on slot machines – under consideration as part of the upcoming budget – would drive punters to illicit market sites that don’t pay tax, contribute to horse racing or exercise regulatory controls. Zarb-Cousin, the director of the gambling-blocking company Gamban and a longtime campaigner for tougher laws, said: “While the UK’s biggest gambling firms have been warning about the risks of growing the illicit market if the government increases tax and regulation, the very same firms are profiting from it. “If the gambling industry is concerned about the black market, it needs to get its own house in order by cutting all ties with it.” A spokesperson for SIS said all of its customers agreed to “only offer SIS products where it is legal to do so and where they have the necessary regulatory licences”. They added: “Customers commit that they will comply with all such laws and licences at all times. “Where SIS becomes aware that these terms are not being adhered to it takes corrective action to enforce the position, up to and including suspension or termination of contracts.” The Guardian approached Evoke and Fred Done for comment. https://praguemonitor.com/pm/czechia/cze.text: Czechia Business Prague Housing Europe & World Work & Life Briefings Key points Ordinary courts have four levels: district, regional, high and the Supreme Court in Brno; the Supreme Administrative Court, also in Brno, hears disputes with public authorities. Which court hears a case first depends on its type and seriousness, and most cases begin at a district court. Judges are appointed by the president, and in the ordinary courts the appointment has no fixed term. On this page 8 sections The ordinary courts A tenancy dispute, step by step Administrative justice Appeals and extraordinary remedies Judges, prosecutors and others Practical points for residents Common misreadings Before any filing Sooner or later, anyone who has signed a Czech tenancy, set up a company or been in a road accident hears a lawyer ask the same question: which court? The answer is rarely the Prague one you might expect. The country's top courts sit in Brno, roughly 200 kilometres from the capital, and the lower courts are organised by territory in a way that follows neither the regions nor the districts exactly. The ordinary courts at a glance Level Court What it does 1 District courts (okresní soudy) Most first-instance cases: consumer claims, tenancies, family, inheritance, minor crime 2 Regional courts (krajské soudy); Municipal Court in Prague Serious crime and larger civil cases at first instance; appeals from district courts 3 High courts (vrchní soudy), in Prague and Olomouc Appeals in cases that began at a regional court 4 Supreme Court (Nejvyšší soud), in Brno Extraordinary remedies; keeps interpretation consistent General outline; the courts' own websites list their territorial jurisdiction. The ordinary courts The ordinary courts handle civil, commercial, family and criminal cases, in a four-level pyramid. District courts ( okresní soudy ) are the entry point for most disputes: consumer claims, tenancies, family matters, inheritance, minor crime. Prague has its own district courts, split among the city's districts. Regional courts ( krajské soudy ) hear the most serious criminal cases and certain larger or specialised civil matters at first instance, and they hear appeals against district court decisions. In Prague the equivalent is the Municipal Court in Prague ( Městský soud v Praze ), which also keeps the commercial register. High courts ( vrchní soudy ) hear appeals in cases that began at a regional court. There are two, in Prague and Olomouc. At the top is the Supreme Court ( Nejvyšší soud ) in Brno. It does not usually re-examine facts. It deals with extraordinary remedies and keeps the interpretation of law consistent across the lower courts. A tenancy dispute, step by step An example makes the pyramid concrete. A tenant and a landlord disagree about the return of a deposit. The claim starts at a district court. Which one depends on the rules of territorial jurisdiction, so a lawyer checks that before filing. One side loses, and appeals to the regional court, in Prague to the Municipal Court. In rare cases that raise an unsettled question of law, an appeal on a point of law can go to the Supreme Court. Beyond that, only a constitutional complaint or the European courts remain, and both require a violation of rights rather than a simple disagreement. A building-permit dispute follows a different route. The owner first appeals within the administration, then brings an action at a regional court sitting in its administrative capacity, then, if the law allows, a cassation complaint to the Supreme Administrative Court. The two ladders never meet, which is why the first question a Czech lawyer asks is whether the dispute is with a person or with an office. Administrative justice Disputes between a person and a public authority go to a separate branch. If you challenge an office's decision on a residence permit, a building permit or a tax assessment, you generally start with the authority's own appeal process. After that you can bring an action before a regional court sitting in its administrative capacity. A cassation complaint can then go to the Supreme Administrative Court ( Nejvyšší správní soud ), also in Brno. This matters for foreigners because many decisions on residence and visas are administrative. Deadlines to bring a case are short (as of 2026; check the official source), and bringing an action does not automatically suspend the decision. Challenging an office's decision Read the instructions at the end of the decision Czech administrative decisions state whether you may appeal, to whom and by when. Appeal within the administration Usually the first step, filed with the office that made the decision. Bring an action in court A regional court in its administrative capacity hears it. Check whether the action suspends the decision (usually it does not). Cassation complaint Possible to the Supreme Administrative Court in Brno on the grounds the law allows. Appeals and extraordinary remedies An ordinary appeal ( odvolání ) lets the next level up reconsider a case, facts included. Extraordinary remedies come after a judgment has become final, and they are limited. The best known is the appeal on a point of law ( dovolání ) to the Supreme Court. It is available only in certain cases, and in civil matters it generally requires a question of law the Supreme Court has not settled, or a departure by the lower court from its case law. Beyond that, a person who has exhausted national remedies can ask the Constitutional Court to review a violation of fundamental rights (see Czech Constitutional Court explained ). After that comes the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg, as in other Council of Europe states. Czech courts can also refer questions of EU law to the Court of Justice of the European Union in Luxembourg. Deadlines run from delivery Most time limits start the day a decision is delivered to you, including by data box. Note the date and keep the envelope or the data-box receipt. How the system took its present shape 1993 Independent Czechia sets up its own Supreme Court and a Constitutional Court, both in Brno 2003 The Supreme Administrative Court begins work in Brno 2004 EU membership: Czech courts can refer questions of EU law to Luxembourg Judges, prosecutors and others Judges are appointed by the president, and in the ordinary courts the appointment has no fixed term. The Ministry of Justice has a formal role in putting judges forward and in appointing court presidents, who manage the courts administratively. The Constitution guarantees judicial independence: a judge is bound by statute and international law, and no ministry can instruct a judge on a ruling. Prosecutors form a separate body. The public prosecution service ( státní zastupitelství ) prepares and brings criminal charges, with a structure that mirrors the courts and the Supreme Public Prosecutor's Office in Brno at the top. Other legal professions have defined roles. Lawyers ( advokáti ) belong to the Czech Bar Association. Notaries handle certain certifications, wills and property documents. Bailiffs ( exekutoři ) enforce court judgments, a field that has been reformed more than once. Practical points for residents Court proceedings are in Czech. The Charter of Fundamental Rights gives anyone who does not speak the language the right to an interpreter, so ask the court how it is arranged. Documents in another language generally need an official translation. Much of the paperwork can be done from home. Filings can be sent through the electronic data box ( datová schránka ), which is mandatory for companies. Court fees depend on the type of claim and are set by law (as of 2026; check the official source). For disputes over housing, employment and contracts, settling outside court is often the quicker route. Czech law provides for mediation, and the Czech Trade Inspection Authority runs out-of-court resolution for consumer disputes. For anything serious, hire a lawyer rather than rely on an article. Common misreadings Newcomers tend to make the same four assumptions. The first is that the Prague courts are the top courts. They are not; Prague has a Municipal Court and a High Court, and the summit is in Brno. The second is that a court of appeal always re-tries the case. Ordinary appeals can reconsider the facts, but extraordinary remedies mostly cannot. The third is that a notary or a bailiff is a kind of judge. Neither is: a notary certifies documents, and a bailiff carries out a judgment the court has already given. The fourth is that the prosecutor and the judge belong to the same chain of command. They do not, and the independence of the bench from the prosecution is one of the basic safeguards of a criminal trial. It also helps to remember that Czech courts decide on written law. Precedent matters, particularly from the highest courts, but a lower court is bound first by statute, which is why the wording of an act matters more in a Czech case than a previous verdict on similar facts. Before any filing Establish which court has jurisdiction. The public administration portal links to the official justice information and the courts' own websites, which list their territorial areas and contact details. Start with the court for your own address, and keep every notice with its date of delivery, because most deadlines run from that date. Frequently asked questions Why are the top courts in Brno and not Prague? Brno hosts the Supreme Court, the Supreme Administrative Court and the Constitutional Court, as well as the Supreme Public Prosecutor's Office. The arrangement is often described as a deliberate decentralisation. Do I get an interpreter in court? The Charter of Fundamental Rights gives anyone who does not speak Czech the right to an interpreter. Ask the court how it is arranged. Can I file by email? Court filings go through approved channels such as the data box; ask the court about the rules for your case.
